decks.title: Fundamentals of Partnership — Part 1: The Firm, the Deed, Capital Accounts and Appropriation of Profit
goals: State the features of partnership and the provisions of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 on books of account and on money matters when the deed is silent
Prepare partners' capital and current accounts, including interest on current-account balances
Prepare the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account with interest on capital, salary, a partner's or manager's commission and reserve

slides.heading: Fundamentals of Partnership
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what a **partnership** is, what the **Act** and the **deed** say, **capital and current accounts**, and the **Profit and Loss Appropriation Account**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: partnership and the Indian Partnership Act, the deed and the rules when there is none, capital and current accounts, and the appropriation of profit
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Welcome to the first chapter of Class twelve Accounts. A large share of Indian businesses, from workshops to clinics, are run by partners who pool money and skill and share the profit. In this part we see what makes a partnership, what the Indian Partnership Act says when partners have not agreed, how capitals are recorded, and how the year's profit is divided.

slides.heading: What is a partnership?
bullets: Section 4 of the **Indian Partnership Act, 1932**: partnership is a relation between persons who have agreed to share the profits of a business carried on by all of them or by any of them acting for all.
Persons who enter into it are **partners**; together they are a **firm**; the business runs under the **firm name**.

headers: In an imagined bamboo-furniture firm in Kohima
rows: At least 2 and at most 50 partners
Neiphiu and Koushik run the workshop together
Oral or written; the written form is the deed
They sign a deed before the first order
A lawful business carried on for profit
Making and selling bamboo chairs and shelves
Profit and loss shared in an agreed ratio
Run by all, or by any of them acting for all
Koushik's order for cane binds Neiphiu too
Partners' own property can meet the firm's debts
A supplier can claim from Neiphiu's savings

visual.alt: Table of six features of partnership with an imagined bamboo-furniture firm in Kohima as the example: two or more persons, an agreement, a business, sharing of profits, mutual agency and unlimited liability

slides.narration: Section four of the Indian Partnership Act describes partnership as a relation between persons who agree to share the profits of a business carried on by all of them, or by any of them acting for all. Six features follow from it. The table shows each one at work in an imagined bamboo furniture workshop run by two friends in Kohima.

slides.heading: The Act on books of account and partners' rights
slides.body_md: Unless the partners agree otherwise, the Act gives every partner these rights and duties.

headers: Provision of the Act (unless partners agree otherwise)
rows: Partners must be just and faithful and give true accounts and full information to each other
Every partner may take part in running the business
Ordinary matters by majority; the nature of the business changes only with every partner's consent
Every partner may have access to, inspect and copy any of the firm's books
Profit sharing, remuneration and interest (next slides)

visual.alt: Table of provisions of the Indian Partnership Act on accounts and partners' rights: true accounts under section nine, the right to take part in the business, decisions by majority, the right to inspect and copy the books, and the money rules of section thirteen

slides.narration: The Act also says how partners deal with each other. Each must be just and faithful and give true accounts and full information. Every partner may take part in the business, ordinary matters go by majority, and every partner, even a sleeping one, may see, inspect and copy the firm's books. Section thirteen then sets the money rules, which we meet next.

slides.heading: The partnership deed
slides.body_md: The written agreement between partners is the **partnership deed**. It is signed by all partners and stamped as the law requires.

rows: Names of the firm and partners; nature and duration of business
Who the partners are and what the firm does
Capital of each partner; fixed or fluctuating capitals
Basis for interest on capital and the type of accounts
Division of the divisible profit or loss
Interest on capital, drawings, current balances and loans
Rates to apply and whether interest is a charge
Rewards and promises to particular partners
Admission, retirement, death, goodwill, disputes, dissolution

visual.alt: Table of the usual clauses of a partnership deed and why each matters to the accountant: names and business, capitals, profit-sharing ratio, interest rates, salary, commission and guarantees, and rules for later changes

slides.narration: Partners usually write their agreement down in a partnership deed. For the accountant it is the rule book: it gives the capitals, the profit-sharing ratio, the rates of interest and whether interest is a charge, the salaries, commissions and any guarantee of profit, and the rules for later changes. A clear deed prevents quarrels at the year end.

slides.heading: When the deed is silent

headers: Rule when the deed is silent (Section 13)
rows: Salary or commission to a partner
Not allowed; where agreed, payable only out of profits
Interest on a partner's loan or advance
6% per annum, a charge (a loan of ₹1,20,000 for 9 months earns ₹5,400)

visual.alt: Table of the rules of section thirteen of the Indian Partnership Act when the deed is silent: equal sharing, no remuneration, no interest on capital, no interest on drawings, and six per cent a year on a partner's loan, so one lakh twenty thousand rupees for nine months earns five thousand four hundred rupees

slides.narration: If there is no deed, or it says nothing on a point, section thirteen of the Act decides. Profits and losses are shared equally. No partner gets salary or commission. No interest is allowed on capital, and where it is agreed it is paid only out of profits. No interest is charged on drawings. But a partner who lends money gets six per cent a year, as a charge.

slides.heading: Quick check: the deed is silent
slides.body_md: Capitals are unequal. Does that change the rule?
slides.narration: Recall which money matter earns six per cent under the Act, and which earns nothing at all.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: settling claims without a deed
slides.body_md: **Kannauj Attar House**, an imagined perfume distillery in Kannauj. Darshan, Gargi and Himmat have no deed. Capitals ₹5,00,000, ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000. Gargi lent the firm ₹1,20,000 on 1 July 2025. Profit for 2025-26 before any interest: ₹2,45,400. Four claims are made at the year end.

rows: Gargi: interest on her loan at 10%
6% a year from 1 July 2025, a charge
Darshan: profit in the capital ratio 5:3:2

visual.alt: Table of worked example one: claims for interest on capital and a salary are refused; Gargi's loan earns six per cent for nine months, five thousand four hundred rupees; the remaining profit of two lakh forty thousand rupees is shared equally, eighty thousand rupees each

slides.narration: Settle each claim by the Act. Interest on capital and a salary need an agreement, so both are refused. Gargi's loan earns six per cent, not ten, and only for nine months: rupees five thousand four hundred, charged before profit is shared. The profit left, rupees two lakh forty thousand, is shared equally, not in the capital ratio: rupees eighty thousand each.

slides.heading: Fixed and fluctuating capitals
columns:
**Fixed capital method**

- Two accounts per partner: **capital** and **current**.
- Capital changes only when capital is added or permanently withdrawn.
- The current account may show a **debit** balance.

**Fluctuating capital method**

- One **capital** account per partner.
- Every adjustment is recorded in it, so its balance moves every year.
- Used when a question does not name a method.

rows: Changes only when capital is added or permanently withdrawn
Possible, though rare, in the capital account

visual.alt: Table comparing the fixed capital method, with separate capital and current accounts, and the fluctuating capital method, with one capital account recording every adjustment

slides.narration: Partners' capitals are kept in one of two ways. Under the fixed capital method, each partner has a capital account that changes only when capital is added or permanently withdrawn, plus a current account for everything else. Under the fluctuating capital method a single capital account records everything. If a question names no method, take capitals as fluctuating.

slides.heading: Where each item goes

rows: Interest on capital and on a credit current balance, salary, commission, share of profit
Drawings, interest on drawings and on a debit current balance, share of loss

visual.alt: Table showing where each item goes: capital brought in or withdrawn goes to the capital account under both methods; earnings are credited and drawings, interest on drawings and losses are debited to the current account under fixed capitals or to the capital account under fluctuating capitals

slides.narration: This map saves marks. Capital brought in or permanently withdrawn always goes to the capital account. Whatever a partner earns from the firm, such as interest, salary, commission and share of profit, is credited. Whatever she takes or is charged, such as drawings, interest on drawings and a share of loss, is debited: to the current account if capitals are fixed, to the capital account if they fluctuate.

slides.heading: Interest on current account balances
bullets: Worked on the **opening** current balance unless the deed says otherwise.
A credit balance earns interest; a debit balance is charged interest.

rows: Allowed: debit P&L Appropriation A/c, credit partner's current account (like interest on capital)
Charged: debit partner's current account, credit P&L Appropriation A/c (like interest on drawings)

visual.alt: Table of interest on current account balances: on a credit balance the firm allows interest like interest on capital; on a debit balance it charges interest like interest on drawings, in each case only if the deed provides

slides.narration: With fixed capitals, some deeds also allow interest on current account balances. A credit balance means the firm owes the partner, so interest is allowed, just like interest on capital. A debit balance means the partner owes the firm, so interest is charged, just like interest on drawings. Both pass through the appropriation account and the partner's current account.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: current accounts with interest on current balances
slides.body_md: **Bhagalpur Silk House**, an imagined firm in Bhagalpur. Eshwar and Jasleen share 3:2; fixed capitals ₹4,00,000 and ₹2,50,000; opening current balances Eshwar ₹30,000 (Cr), Jasleen ₹10,000 (Dr). Interest on capital 8%, on current balances 6%; Jasleen's salary ₹3,000 a month; drawings ₹45,000 and ₹30,000; interest on drawings ₹1,350 and ₹900; net profit ₹1,95,000.
bullets: Interest on current balances: Eshwar allowed ₹1,800, Jasleen charged ₹600.
Divisible profit ₹1,08,050: Eshwar ₹64,830, Jasleen ₹43,220.

visual.alt: Current accounts of Eshwar and Jasleen: Eshwar opens with a credit and Jasleen with a debit balance; interest, salary and profit are credited and drawings and interest on drawings debited; closing credit balances eighty two thousand two hundred eighty and fifty seven thousand seven hundred twenty rupees
visual.caption: Capitals stay at ₹4,00,000 and ₹2,50,000.

slides.narration: Eshwar's credit balance earns six per cent, rupees one thousand eight hundred; Jasleen's debit balance is charged rupees six hundred. After interest on capital and Jasleen's salary, the divisible profit is rupees one lakh eight thousand fifty, shared three to two. Post everything to the current accounts: Jasleen's opening debit sits on the debit side. Eshwar closes at rupees eighty two thousand two hundred eighty and Jasleen at rupees fifty seven thousand seven hundred twenty.

slides.heading: Quick check: a current account in debit
slides.body_md: Think of a partner who takes out more than the firm credits to him.
slides.narration: Ask which account receives drawings when capitals are fixed, and what happens when they exceed the year's credits.

slides.heading: The Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
bullets: It starts from the **net profit** after all charges.
Its two sides must total the same.

rows: By Profit and Loss A/c (net profit, after charges)
To Interest on credit current balances
By Interest on debit current balances
To Partners' Capital or Current A/cs (divisible profit in the ratio)

visual.alt: Format of the profit and loss appropriation account: debit interest on capital and on credit current balances, partners' salary and commission, transfer to reserve and the shares of divisible profit; credit the net profit, interest on drawings and interest on debit current balances
visual.caption: Divisible profit = net profit + interest on drawings − interest on capital − salary − commission − reserve

slides.narration: The appropriation account divides the net profit found after all charges. On the credit side go the net profit, interest on drawings and interest on any debit current balances. On the debit side go interest on capital and on credit current balances, partners' salaries and commission, and transfers to reserve. The rest is the divisible profit, shared in the profit-sharing ratio.

slides.heading: Interest on capital
bullets: On the **opening** capital for the year; on additions from their date; reduced for capital withdrawn from its date.

rows: Deed allows interest; profit is enough
Same, but profit is less than the interest due
Whole profit shared in the ratio of interest due
Same, but the firm made a loss
No interest (Section 13: only out of profits)
Deed treats interest as a charge
Full interest debited to the Profit and Loss Account, even if this causes a loss

visual.alt: Table of the treatment of interest on capital: none if the deed is silent; full interest out of enough profit; the profit shared in the interest ratio when it is short; none in a loss year; full interest as a charge when the deed says so

slides.narration: Interest on capital runs on the opening capital for the year, on additions from the date they come in, and stops on capital withdrawn from that date. As an appropriation it is paid only out of profit, as section thirteen says: when profit falls short, the whole profit is shared in the ratio of interest due, and in a loss year nothing is allowed. As a charge it is allowed in full.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: when profit falls short
slides.body_md: **Majuli Mask Studio**, an imagined firm on Majuli. Ketaki and Bhupen share 3:2. Capitals on 1 April 2025: ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,40,000; Ketaki added ₹60,000 on 1 October 2025; Bhupen withdrew ₹40,000 of capital on 1 January 2026. Interest on capital 10% a year. Net profit ₹44,800. Show (a) interest as an appropriation, (b) the same in a loss year, (c) interest as a charge.

rows: (c) Charge: full interest, loss of 11,200 shared 3:2

visual.alt: Table of worked example three: interest due is thirty three thousand for Ketaki and twenty three thousand for Bhupen; as an appropriation the profit of forty four thousand eight hundred is shared twenty six thousand four hundred and eighteen thousand four hundred; in a loss year nothing is allowed; as a charge full interest is credited and a loss of eleven thousand two hundred rupees is shared three to two

slides.narration: Ketaki's interest is ten per cent on her opening capital plus six months on the addition: rupees thirty three thousand. Bhupen's is a full year on his opening capital less three months on the amount withdrawn: rupees twenty three thousand. As an appropriation, the profit is shared in the ratio of interest due. In a loss year, no interest. As a charge, full interest is allowed and the loss of rupees eleven thousand two hundred is shared three to two.

slides.heading: Quick check: profit short of interest
slides.body_md: Here interest on capital is an appropriation.
slides.narration: Remember how the mask studio shared its profit when it could not cover the interest due.

slides.heading: Salary and commission: partner or manager?
bullets: A partner gets salary or commission **only if the deed provides**: an **appropriation**.
A **manager** is an employee: his commission is a **charge**, found before net profit.
Read whether commission is on profit **before** or **after** charging it.

visual.alt: Flow for commissions: from a profit of four lakh sixty two thousand rupees the manager's commission after charging, ten over one hundred and ten, is forty two thousand rupees, a charge; the net profit of four lakh twenty thousand rupees then carries the partner's commission of twenty one thousand rupees as an appropriation
visual.caption: After charging: profit × rate ÷ (100 + rate). Before charging: profit × rate ÷ 100.

slides.narration: A partner gets salary or commission only if the deed provides, and it is an appropriation. A manager is an employee, so his commission is a charge, taken before the net profit is found. If commission is on profit after charging that commission, divide by one hundred plus the rate. Always read whose profit the commission is calculated on.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: the manager comes first
slides.body_md: **Kollam Cashew Works**, an imagined firm in Kollam. Rukmini, Sudhir and Vinod share 2:2:1. Profit before the manager's commission ₹4,62,000; the manager gets 10% of net profit **after** charging his commission.

rows: By Profit and Loss A/c (profit before manager's commission)
To P&L Appropriation A/c (net profit transferred)

visual.alt: Profit and loss adjustment account of Kollam Cashew Works: the manager's commission of forty two thousand rupees is debited and the net profit of four lakh twenty thousand rupees transferred to the appropriation account

slides.narration: The manager is paid before the partners. Ten per cent after charging means rupees four lakh sixty two thousand times ten, divided by one hundred and ten: rupees forty two thousand. That is exactly ten per cent of what remains. It is debited in the profit and loss adjustment account, and the net profit of rupees four lakh twenty thousand goes to the appropriation account.

slides.heading: Worked example 4 (contd): the appropriation account
slides.body_md: Capitals ₹5,00,000, ₹4,00,000, ₹3,00,000 at 6%; Vinod's salary ₹4,000 a month; Sudhir's commission 5% of the net profit; reserve ₹30,000; interest on drawings ₹2,400, ₹1,800, ₹1,200.

rows: By Profit and Loss A/c (net profit)
To Rukmini's Capital A/c (share of profit)
To Sudhir's Capital A/c (share of profit)
To Vinod's Capital A/c (share of profit)

visual.alt: Profit and loss appropriation account of Kollam Cashew Works: net profit and interest on drawings credited; interest on capital, Vinod's salary, Sudhir's commission, the reserve and shares of one lakh one thousand seven hundred sixty, one lakh one thousand seven hundred sixty and fifty thousand eight hundred eighty rupees debited
visual.caption: Divisible profit ₹2,54,400 shared 2:2:1.

slides.narration: Start from the net profit of rupees four lakh twenty thousand and add interest on drawings. Debit interest on capital at six per cent, Vinod's salary, Sudhir's commission of rupees twenty one thousand, and the reserve. The divisible profit of rupees two lakh fifty four thousand four hundred is shared two to two to one: rupees one lakh one thousand seven hundred sixty each to Rukmini and Sudhir and rupees fifty thousand eight hundred eighty to Vinod.

slides.heading: Quick check: commission after charging
slides.body_md: Use the after-charging formula.
slides.narration: Divide by one hundred plus the rate, then check that your answer is the rate on what is left.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Agreement to share the profits of a business carried on by all or any of them acting for all; 2 to 50 partners
True accounts; every partner may inspect and copy the books
Equal profits; no remuneration; no interest on capital or drawings; 6% on partners' advances
Fixed: capital and current accounts. Fluctuating: one capital account
Credit balance: allowed. Debit balance: charged. Only if the deed says so
Appropriation: out of profit only, in the interest ratio if short. Charge: always
Manager: a charge. Partner: an appropriation. After charging: × rate ÷ (100 + rate)

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: the definition of partnership, the Act on books, the rules when the deed is silent, the two capital methods, interest on current balances, interest on capital and the treatment of commission

slides.narration: To sum up. A partnership rests on an agreement, best written as a deed; where the deed is silent, section thirteen of the Act applies. Capitals are fixed, with current accounts, or fluctuating. The appropriation account divides the net profit after charges, allowing interest, salary, commission and reserve before the divisible profit is shared.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Read the deed first: is interest on capital an **appropriation** or a **charge**?
A **manager's** commission is a charge; a **partner's** is an appropriation.
Interest on additions runs from their date; on withdrawals it stops from theirs: write the months.
Interest on a **debit** current balance is credited to the appropriation account.
Total both sides of every account before moving on.
slides.narration: Examiners award step marks, so show working notes for interest, commission and the divisible profit. Common slips are putting a manager's commission in the appropriation account, charging interest on additional capital for the whole year, allowing interest on capital in a loss year when it is not a charge, and putting interest on a debit current balance on the wrong side.

decks.title: Fundamentals of Partnership — Part 2: Charges, Interest on Drawings, Guarantee and Past Adjustments
goals: Distinguish charges against profit (interest on a partner's loan, rent to a partner) from appropriations and record them through the Profit and Loss Adjustment Account
Calculate interest on drawings by the product method and the average-period method
Record a guaranteed minimum profit borne by one or more partners, and correct past omissions with one adjustment entry

slides.heading: Charges, drawings, guarantees and past adjustments
slides.body_md: Part 2 — **charges** against profit, **interest on drawings**, **guarantee** of profits and **past adjustments**.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: charges against profit, interest on drawings, guarantee of profits to a partner, and past adjustments
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part two we first separate the firm's expenses that involve partners from the division of profit. Then we charge interest on what partners withdraw. Next we see what happens when a partner is promised a minimum profit. Finally we correct mistakes that are found only after the accounts have been closed.

slides.heading: Charge or appropriation?

headers: Charge against profit (Profit and Loss Account)
rows: Interest on capital (unless the deed calls it a charge)
Rent paid to a partner for the firm's premises
Salary or commission to a partner
Allowed even in a year of loss

visual.alt: Two-column table: charges such as interest on a partner's loan, rent paid to a partner and a manager's commission go to the profit and loss account even in a loss year; appropriations such as interest on capital, partners' salary or commission and reserves come out of profit only

slides.narration: A charge is an expense the firm would bear whoever the other party was. Interest on a partner's loan, rent for a partner's building and a manager's commission are charges, debited before the net profit is found, even in a loss year. Interest on capital, partners' salary and commission and transfers to reserve are appropriations: they share out a profit that already exists.

slides.heading: Worked example 5: charges first
slides.body_md: **Firozabad Glassworks**, an imagined bangle maker in Firozabad. Mohini and Navneet share 3:2. Profit for 2025-26 before the items below: ₹3,10,000. Navneet lent ₹2,00,000 on 1 October 2025, with no rate agreed. The firm uses Mohini's warehouse at ₹5,000 a month.

rows: To Interest on Navneet's Loan (6% for 6 months)
By Profit and Loss A/c (profit before the charges below)
To P&L Appropriation A/c (net profit transferred)

visual.alt: Profit and loss adjustment account of Firozabad Glassworks: interest on Navneet's loan of six thousand rupees and rent to Mohini of sixty thousand rupees are debited, leaving a net profit of two lakh forty four thousand rupees

slides.narration: With no rate agreed, Navneet's loan earns the Act's six per cent, and only for six months: rupees six thousand. Rent to Mohini for the year is rupees sixty thousand. Both are charges, so they go to the profit and loss adjustment account, leaving a net profit of rupees two lakh forty four thousand for the appropriation account.

slides.heading: Worked example 5 (contd): then appropriations
slides.body_md: Capitals ₹6,00,000 and ₹4,00,000 earn interest at 5%; Mohini's salary is ₹24,000 a year.

rows: By Profit and Loss A/c (net profit)
To Mohini's Capital A/c (share of profit)
To Navneet's Capital A/c (share of profit)

visual.alt: Profit and loss appropriation account of Firozabad Glassworks: from the net profit of two lakh forty four thousand rupees, interest on capital and Mohini's salary are debited and the divisible profit of one lakh seventy thousand rupees is shared three to two

slides.narration: Now divide the net profit. Interest on capital at five per cent and Mohini's salary are debited. The divisible profit of rupees one lakh seventy thousand is shared three to two: rupees one lakh two thousand to Mohini and rupees sixty eight thousand to Navneet. Notice that Mohini receives rent and salary in two different accounts.

slides.heading: Quick check: rent to a partner
slides.body_md: Would the firm pay this to any landlord?
slides.narration: Decide whether the rent is an expense of running the firm or a way of dividing its profit.

slides.heading: Interest on drawings: when and how
bullets: Charged only if the **deed provides**; credited to the appropriation account.
Different amounts or dates: **product method**. Equal amounts at equal gaps: **average period**.

visual.alt: Table of average periods: monthly drawings give six and a half, six or five and a half months; quarterly drawings seven and a half, six or four and a half; half-yearly nine, six or three months, for drawings at the beginning, middle or end of each period
visual.caption: Average period = (months left after the first drawing + months left after the last) ÷ 2. No dates given: 6 months.

slides.narration: Interest on drawings is charged only if the deed says so. When amounts or dates differ, use the product method. When equal amounts are drawn at equal gaps, use an average period: the months left after the first drawing plus the months left after the last, divided by two. If no dates are given, charge interest for six months.

visual.caption: First drawing 12 months, last 1 month: (12 + 1) ÷ 2 = 6½.

slides.narration: Here is why monthly drawings at the beginning of each month use six and a half months. The April drawing stays out for twelve months, May for eleven, and so on down to March, for just one month. The average of twelve and one is six and a half. Drawings at the end of each month run from eleven months down to none, so the average is five and a half.

slides.heading: Worked example 6: the product method
slides.body_md: **Bhadohi Carpet House**, an imagined firm in Bhadohi. Partner Waheeda's drawings in 2025-26 were: ₹12,000 on 1 May 2025; ₹9,000 on 31 August 2025; ₹15,000 on 1 December 2025; ₹6,000 on 28 February 2026. Interest on drawings is 8% a year; the year ends on 31 March 2026.

visual.alt: Product method table for Waheeda's four drawings: products total two lakh sixty one thousand; interest at eight per cent for one month on this total is one thousand seven hundred forty rupees
visual.caption: Interest = 2,61,000 × 8/100 × 1/12 = ₹1,740

slides.narration: Count the months from each drawing to the year end: eleven, seven, four and one. Multiply each amount by its months and add the products, giving rupees two lakh sixty one thousand. That total is like one month's borrowing, so interest is eight per cent for one month on it: rupees one thousand seven hundred forty.

slides.heading: Guarantee of profits to a partner
bullets: Guarantee by the **firm**: the other partners bear the deficiency in their mutual ratio.
Guarantee by **one partner**: that partner bears all of it.
Guarantee by **some partners**: they bear it in the ratio they agreed.

nodes.label: Divide the profit in the normal ratio
Compare the guaranteed partner's share with the minimum
Deficiency borne by the guarantors in their agreed ratio

visual.alt: Flow for a guarantee of minimum profit: divide the profit normally, compare the guaranteed partner's share with the minimum, find the deficiency, and charge it to whoever gave the guarantee in the ratio they agreed
visual.caption: The firm's total profit never changes.

slides.narration: A partner may be promised that her share will not fall below a fixed amount. Divide the profit normally first. If her share is below the minimum, the gap is the deficiency. Whoever gave the guarantee fills it: the other partners in their own ratio if the firm guaranteed, one partner alone if he did, or two partners in whatever ratio they agreed.

slides.heading: Past adjustments
bullets: Typical errors: interest on capital or drawings omitted or at a wrong rate, salary omitted, profit shared in the wrong ratio.
Fixed capitals: **current** accounts. Fluctuating capitals: **capital** accounts.

nodes.label: Error found after the accounts are closed
What each partner should have been credited or debited
Less what was actually credited or debited

visual.alt: Flow for a past adjustment: after the accounts are closed, list what each partner should have received, subtract what was actually recorded, find each net effect, which total nil, and pass one adjustment entry
visual.caption: Closed accounts are never reopened.

slides.narration: Sometimes, after the books are closed, the partners find that interest or a salary was left out, or the profit was shared in the wrong ratio. The accounts are not reopened. Instead a table shows, for each partner, what should have been credited less what was credited. The net effects always total nil, and one entry puts them right.

slides.body_md: **Tezpur Tea Brokers**, an imagined firm in Tezpur. Neelam, Mehul and Suhail share 2:1:1 with fluctuating capitals of ₹3,00,000, ₹2,00,000, ₹1,00,000 on 1 April 2025. After the 2025-26 profit was distributed, they found that interest on capital at 8% a year and Suhail's salary of ₹2,000 a month had been omitted.

visual.alt: Past adjustment table for Neelam, Mehul and Suhail: interest on capital and Suhail's salary credited, the total of seventy two thousand taken back two to one to one; net effect Neelam debit twelve thousand, Mehul debit two thousand, Suhail credit fourteen thousand rupees, totalling nil

slides.narration: Credit each partner with the omitted interest, and Suhail with his salary. Together these are rupees seventy two thousand that should have come out of the profit before it was shared, so take that sum back in two to one to one. Adding each column, Neelam loses rupees twelve thousand, Mehul loses rupees two thousand and Suhail gains rupees fourteen thousand.

Because the capitals fluctuate, the entry goes through the capital accounts. Only if the deed provides; product method, or average period = (first + last) ÷ 2

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 2: charges against profit, interest on drawings, who bears a deficiency under each kind of guarantee including a loss year, and the rule for past adjustments

slides.narration: To sum up. Charges such as interest on a partner's loan, rent to a partner and a manager's commission are met before net profit. Interest on drawings uses the product method or an average period. A guarantee moves a deficiency to the guarantors without changing the firm's profit. Past errors are corrected with one entry built from a table whose net effects total nil.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Prepare a **Profit and Loss Adjustment Account** whenever charges are given after the profit figure.
Count months for drawings to the **year end**; with no dates, use **6 months**.
In guarantee questions, write **who** guaranteed and in **what ratio** before dividing.
A guarantee holds in a **loss** year too: deficiency = minimum + share of loss.
Total the net-effect row of a past adjustment: it **must be nil**.
slides.narration: In the exam, read the guarantee clause twice: the guarantors and their agreed ratio decide everything. Show a profit and loss adjustment account when charges are listed after the profit. For drawings, count months to the year end. In past adjustments, if the net effects do not total nil, recheck the table before writing the entry.

key_terms.definition_md: The partners collectively; the business is carried on under the firm name.

sections.heading: 3. Capital and current accounts
sections.body_md:
**Fixed capital method:** two accounts per partner.
- **Capital account:** opening capital, additional capital (credit), capital permanently withdrawn (debit). Always a credit balance.
- **Current account:** interest on capital, salary, commission, share of profit, interest on a credit current balance (credit); drawings, interest on drawings, share of loss, interest on a debit current balance (debit). May have a debit balance.

**Fluctuating capital method:** one capital account per partner records every item; its balance changes every year. Use it when a question names no method.

**Interest on current balances** (only if the deed provides): allowed on a credit balance like interest on capital; charged on a debit balance like interest on drawings; both through the appropriation account.

**Opening capital from closing capital:** closing capital + drawings + interest on drawings + share of loss − share of profit − interest on capital − salary − commission − additional capital = opening capital.

sections.heading: 5. Charges against profit and interest on drawings
sections.body_md:
**Charges** are met before net profit, even in a loss year: interest on a partner's loan (6% if no rate is agreed), rent paid to a partner, a manager's commission. When the profit is given before such items, prepare a **Profit and Loss Adjustment Account**: credit the profit, debit the charges, and transfer the net profit to the appropriation account.

**Interest on drawings** is charged only if the deed provides; it is debited to the partner and credited to the appropriation account.
- **Product method:** multiply each drawing by the months left to the year end; interest = total of products × rate ÷ 100 × 1/12.
- **Average period** for equal drawings at equal gaps = (months left after the first drawing + months left after the last) ÷ 2. Whole year: monthly 6½ / 6 / 5½ (beginning / middle / end); quarterly 7½ / 6 / 4½; half-yearly 9 / 6 / 3.
- Dates not given: 6 months.

sections.heading: 7. Past adjustments
sections.body_md:
Errors or omissions found **after** the accounts are closed (interest on capital or drawings omitted or at a wrong rate, salary or commission omitted, a wrong profit-sharing ratio) are corrected without reopening the accounts.

**Method:**
1. For each partner, list what should have been credited (+) or debited (−).
2. Deduct what was actually credited: when appropriations were omitted, take their total back in the profit-sharing ratio; for a wrong ratio, compare the right and wrong shares.
3. Find the **net effect** for each partner; the net effects total **nil**.
4. Pass one entry: debit the partners who lose, credit those who gain (current accounts if capitals are fixed, capital accounts if fluctuating), and post it to give the adjusted capitals.

When interest on capital is omitted and opening capitals are not given, work them back from the closing capitals first.

Admission of a manager as a partner is not in the ISC 2027 syllabus for guarantee or past-adjustment problems.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**How marks are usually split (ISC Accounts, Section A)**
- 1 mark: one correct option, a term or a short reason.
- 2 marks: one computation with its working, such as interest on drawings, a commission or a single adjustment entry.
- 3 marks: a short account or working table, such as a small appropriation account, a past-adjustment table with its entry or interest with additions and withdrawals.
- 5 marks: a full Profit and Loss Adjustment and Appropriation Account, current accounts, or a guarantee or past-adjustment problem with adjusted capitals.

**Common mistakes**
- Putting interest on a partner's loan, rent to a partner or a manager's commission in the appropriation account (they are charges).
- Charging the Act's 6% on a loan for the full year when it was given during the year.
- Allowing interest on capital in a loss year when the deed does not call it a charge.
- Charging interest on an addition to capital for the whole year, or ignoring a withdrawal.
- Treating interest on a debit current balance as an expense of the firm.
- Counting drawing months to the wrong date, or forgetting 6 months when dates are not given.
- Letting the guaranteed partner bear part of his own deficiency, or using the profit ratio when the guarantors agreed another ratio.
- A past-adjustment table whose net effects do not total nil.

All firms and figures in SOYL practice are imagined; the board paper will give its own.

questions.stem_md: Which one of the following is **not** an element of the definition of partnership in Section 4 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932?

options.text_md: An agreement between the persons concerned
Registration of the firm with the Registrar of Firms
A business whose profits are to be shared
The business carried on by all the partners or by any of them acting for all

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Registration of the firm with the Registrar of Firms. Registration is optional; an unregistered firm only loses certain rights to sue. The other three are taken from the definition itself.

questions.stem_md: Gulzar is a sleeping partner in an imagined spice-trading firm in Bikaner whose deed says nothing about the books. He asks to see the cash book and ledger, and the working partners refuse. Under Section 12 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, Gulzar

options.text_md: may see the books only if he works in the business
may see the final accounts, but not the books
has no right to the books unless the deed gives him one
may have access to, inspect and copy any of the books of the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** may have access to, inspect and copy any of the books of the firm. Unless the partners have agreed otherwise, Section 12(d) lets every partner, active or sleeping, have access to the firm's books and inspect and copy them.

questions.stem_md: Hemlata, a partner in an imagined pickle-making firm in Palakkad, buys raw mangoes on credit for the firm without asking her partners. The supplier now asks the firm to pay. The firm is bound to pay mainly because of

options.text_md: mutual agency: Hemlata acted for the firm in its ordinary business
the unlimited liability of the partners
the profit-sharing ratio in the deed
the registration of the firm

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** mutual agency: Hemlata acted for the firm in its ordinary business. An act of a partner in the ordinary course of the firm's business binds the firm and every partner. Unlimited liability decides whose property can meet a debt once the firm owes it; it does not create the debt.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A partnership firm comes into existence only on the day it is registered with the Registrar of Firms under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The partnership arises from the agreement among the partners. Registration is optional, although an unregistered firm cannot sue an outsider to enforce a contract.

questions.stem_md: Because of mutual agency, each partner of a firm is an agent of the other partners and is also their ___ .
questions.solution_md: Each partner is both an agent (his acts bind the others) and a principal (he is bound by their acts).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** If the assets of a partnership firm cannot pay all its creditors, the creditors may recover the balance from the private property of any partner.

**Reason (R):** Every partner of a firm has unlimited liability and is liable, jointly with the others and also severally, for all acts of the firm.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both statements are true, and the unlimited, joint and several liability in R is exactly why a creditor can reach a partner's own property.

questions.stem_md: Mridula lends ₹3,00,000 to an imagined organic-jaggery business in Muzaffarnagar run by her friend Kamini. Instead of a fixed rate of interest, Kamini agrees to pay her 10% of each year's profit. Mridula takes no part in the business and cannot sign for it. Is Mridula a partner? Give two reasons.
questions.solution_md: Test the relationship against the definition, not against the profit share alone.

answer.model_answer_md:
**No, Mridula is not a partner.**
1. Receiving a share of profit is not conclusive proof of partnership: a lender may be paid out of profits, and her 10% is simply the reward for her loan.
2. There is no agreement that the business is carried on by both of them or by Kamini acting for both, so there is no mutual agency: Kamini cannot bind Mridula, and Mridula cannot bind the business.

marking_scheme.step: Profit share is not conclusive; she is a lender
No agreement to carry on the business jointly and no mutual agency

questions.stem_md: Unless partners agree otherwise, what do Sections 9 and 12 of the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 say about the firm's books and a partner's part in the business? State **two** provisions.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each correct provision.

answer.model_answer_md:
Any two of:
1. Every partner has a right to have access to, inspect and copy any of the books of the firm (Section 12).
2. Every partner has a right to take part in the conduct of the business (Section 12).
3. Partners must render true accounts and full information of everything affecting the firm to any partner (Section 9).
4. Ordinary matters are decided by a majority of partners, but the nature of the business cannot be changed without the consent of all (Section 12).

questions.stem_md: Anirban, Lavanya and Udit start an imagined drone-survey business in Hubballi as partners. With reference to their business, explain **five** essential features of a partnership.
questions.solution_md: Each feature needs its meaning and a link to the drone-survey business; any five of the six.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Two or more persons:** Anirban, Lavanya and Udit are three persons; a firm may have at least two and at most fifty partners.
2. **Agreement:** they are partners because they agreed to be, orally or in a written deed; a partnership cannot arise from status or birth.
3. **Lawful business:** the agreement is to carry on a business, here surveying land and buildings with drones for clients.
4. **Sharing of profits:** they agree to share the profits, and losses, of the survey business in an agreed ratio (equally if nothing is agreed).
5. **Mutual agency:** the business may be carried on by all three or by any one of them acting for all; a contract Udit signs with a client binds Anirban and Lavanya too.
6. **Unlimited liability:** if the firm cannot pay for a drone bought on credit, the seller can recover from the private property of any partner.

questions.stem_md: Sanya and Trisha run an imagined translation bureau in Puducherry without any partnership deed. Sanya's capital is three times Trisha's. Under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932, interest on their capitals is

options.text_md: allowed at 6% per annum to both partners
allowed only to Sanya, as the larger contributor
not allowed to either partner
allowed at 6% per annum, but only out of profits

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** not allowed to either partner. The Act gives no interest on capital unless the partners agree to it, whatever the capitals. The 6% rate belongs to a partner's loan or advance, not to capital.

questions.stem_md: Chaitanya, a partner in an imagined sports-goods firm in Jalandhar, advanced ₹1,50,000 to the firm on 1 August 2025, over and above his capital. There is no deed and no agreement on interest. For the year ended 31 March 2026, the firm's Profit and Loss Account should be debited with interest on this advance of

options.text_md: nil, because there is no deed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** ₹6,000. The Act allows 6% a year on a partner's advance from the date it is made: ₹1,50,000 × 6/100 × 8/12 = ₹6,000. A full year would wrongly give ₹9,000.

questions.stem_md: Four disputes arise in an imagined handloom firm in Bishnupur that has no partnership deed. Match each situation with the way the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 settles it.

options.text_md: Damini works twelve hours a day; her partners rarely visit the looms
Eklavya brought in twice as much capital as each of the others
Falguni lent the firm cash beyond her capital
Girish withdrew cash every month for household use

match_right.text_md: No interest is charged on his drawings
No salary or commission for her work
Interest at 6% a year, even in a loss year

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). With the deed silent: no remuneration, equal sharing, 6% a year on advances as a charge, and no interest on drawings.

questions.stem_md: True or false? When a partnership deed says nothing about interest on capital, each partner is allowed interest on capital at 6% per annum under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** The 6% rate applies only to loans or advances made by a partner. Interest on capital is not allowed at all unless the partners agree to it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Partners are well advised to set out the terms of their partnership in a written deed, signed by every partner and properly stamped.

**Reason (R):** A partnership cannot come into existence unless the agreement between the partners is in writing.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: a written deed prevents disputes and is good evidence of the terms. R is false: an oral agreement is enough to create a partnership.

questions.stem_md: Two partners of an imagined dental clinic in Kannur have only an oral understanding. Give **two** reasons why they should draw up a written partnership deed.
questions.solution_md: One mark for each well-explained reason.

answer.model_answer_md:
Any two of:
1. It records the terms (capital, profit-sharing ratio, interest, salaries, drawings) clearly, so disputes can be settled by referring to it.
2. It is reliable evidence of the agreement before a court or arbitrator.
3. It sets the rules for later events such as admission, retirement or death of a partner and dissolution.
4. It is needed when the firm applies for registration, a bank loan or a tax registration.

questions.stem_md: Jeevan and Ruksana run an imagined toy-making workshop in Kondapalli with no partnership deed. Their capitals are ₹4,00,000 and ₹1,00,000, and Ruksana lent the workshop ₹80,000 on 1 April 2025. The profit for 2025-26 before any interest is ₹1,26,000. Jeevan wants interest on capital at 8% and profit shared in the capital ratio; Ruksana wants interest on her loan at 12%. Settle the claims and find each partner's share of profit.
questions.solution_md: Apply the Act's default rules: interest on the loan first, as a charge, and then equal division.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Interest on capital:** not allowed, as there is no agreement to pay it.
2. **Interest on Ruksana's loan:** 6% a year, not 12%: ₹80,000 × 6/100 = ₹4,800, a charge against profit.
3. **Profit sharing:** equal, not in the capital ratio. Profit after the loan interest = ₹1,26,000 − ₹4,800 = ₹1,21,200; each partner gets **₹60,600**.

marking_scheme.step: Interest on capital refused with reason
Loan interest ₹4,800 at 6% as a charge
Equal shares of the remaining profit

questions.stem_md: Bhaskar and his cousin Keya are drafting a partnership deed for an imagined cloud kitchen in Dharamshala. Suggest **six** clauses their deed should contain.
questions.solution_md: Any six relevant clauses; one mark for every two.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Name and address of the firm and of each partner, and the nature of the business.
2. Date of commencement and duration of the partnership.
3. Capital to be contributed by each partner.
4. Profit-sharing ratio.
5. Rates of interest on capital, on drawings and on partners' loans.
6. Salary or commission to working partners.
7. Method of keeping accounts and preparing the final accounts each year.
8. Rules for admission, retirement and death of a partner, valuation of goodwill, settlement of disputes and dissolution.

questions.stem_md: Rehana, Sukhmani and Wangchuk run an imagined trekking-gear rental firm in Kullu. They have no partnership deed. Their capitals are ₹6,00,000, ₹4,00,000, ₹2,00,000. Rehana also lent the firm ₹2,40,000 on 1 October 2025. The profit for the year ended 31 March 2026, before any of the items below, is ₹2,79,000. At the year end: (i) Wangchuk, who works full time, claims a salary of ₹10,000 per month; (ii) Rehana claims interest on capital at 10% and interest on her loan at 12% per annum; (iii) Sukhmani wants the profit divided in the capital ratio. (a) Settle each claim, giving reasons. (b) Prepare the Profit and Loss Adjustment Account and show each partner's share of profit.
questions.solution_md: Reject what the Act does not give, charge the loan interest from its date, then divide the rest equally.

answer.model_answer_md:
**(a) Claims under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932**

1. Salary to Wangchuk: **not allowed**; no partner is entitled to remuneration without an agreement.

2. Interest on capital to Rehana: **not allowed** without an agreement.

3. Interest on Rehana's loan: **6%** per annum, not 12%, from 1 October 2025: ₹2,40,000 × 6/100 × 6/12 = ₹7,200. It is a charge against profit.

4. Division of profit: **equal**, whatever the capitals; Sukhmani's claim fails.

**(b) Profit and Loss Adjustment Account** for the year ended 31 March 2026

| Dr: Particulars | ₹ | Cr: Particulars | ₹ |
|---|---|---|---|
| To Interest on Rehana's Loan (6% for 6 months) | 7,200 | By Profit and Loss A/c (profit before the charges below) | 2,79,000 |
| To P&L Appropriation A/c (net profit transferred) | 2,71,800 |  |  |
|  | **2,79,000** |  | **2,79,000** |

Net profit ₹2,71,800 shared equally: Rehana, Sukhmani and Wangchuk **₹90,600** each.

marking_scheme.step: Salary and interest on capital claims refused with reasons
Equal shares of the net profit

questions.stem_md: Partners of an imagined lock-making firm in Aligarh keep their capitals **fixed**. The salary allowed to a working partner for the year is credited to her

options.text_md: current account
capital account
loan account
drawings account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** current account. With fixed capitals every routine item of the year, including salary, interest and share of profit, passes through the current account; the capital account changes only for capital brought in or permanently withdrawn.

questions.stem_md: When a firm follows the **fluctuating** capital method, each partner's capital is recorded in

options.text_md: a capital account and a current account
a capital account and a loan account
the Balance Sheet only, without a ledger account
one capital account, which records every adjustment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** one capital account, which records every adjustment. Under the fluctuating method, interest, salary, profit and drawings are all recorded in the single capital account, so its balance changes every year.

questions.stem_md: The deed of an imagined firm with fixed capitals allows interest at 5% per annum on the opening balances of partners' current accounts, whether credit or debit. On 1 April 2025 Harshita's current account showed a **debit** balance of ₹24,000. The interest of ₹1,200 for 2025-26 is

options.text_md: credited to Harshita's current account and debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
debited to Harshita's current account and credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account
debited to Harshita's capital account and credited to the Profit and Loss Account
ignored, because interest is never charged on a current account

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** debited to Harshita's current account and credited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account. A debit balance means Harshita owes the firm, so the interest is charged to her, like interest on drawings: ₹24,000 × 5/100 = ₹1,200, debited to her current account and credited to the appropriation account.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Avinash's capital account in an imagined firm with fixed capitals shows a credit of ₹2,00,000. After a year of heavy drawings and a small profit, his current account can show a debit balance while his capital account still shows that credit.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Drawings and interest on them go to the current account; if they exceed his interest, salary and share of profit, the current account goes into debit. The capital account is untouched.

questions.stem_md: In a firm whose capitals are fixed, a partner's drawings and the interest charged on them are debited to his ___ account.
questions.solution_md: They go to the current account; only permanent changes in capital pass through the capital account.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Under the fluctuating capital method, a partner's capital account can never show a debit balance.

**Reason (R):** Under the fluctuating capital method, drawings, interest, salary and the share of profit or loss are all recorded in the partner's capital account.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false: heavy drawings or a share of loss recorded in the single capital account can push it into debit. R is true, and is the reason the balance fluctuates.

questions.stem_md: Dolma is a partner in an imagined carpet-weaving firm in Mirzapur that keeps **fluctuating** capitals. Her capital on 1 April 2025 was ₹2,50,000. For 2025-26 she is allowed interest on capital at 10% and a salary of ₹1,500 per month, and her share of profit is ₹42,000. She withdrew ₹30,000 and is charged interest on drawings of ₹900. Find her capital on 31 March 2026 (in ₹).
questions.solution_md: 2,50,000 + 25,000 (interest) + 18,000 (salary) + 42,000 (profit) − 30,000 (drawings) − 900 (interest on drawings) = ₹3,04,100.

questions.stem_md: An imagined firm in Darbhanga must choose between keeping its partners' capitals fixed or fluctuating. Distinguish between the two methods on any **two** bases.
questions.solution_md: Any two bases, each contrasted for both methods.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Fixed capital method | Fluctuating capital method |
|---|---|---|
| Number of accounts | Two for each partner: capital and current | One for each partner: capital |
| Routine items (interest, salary, profit, drawings) | Recorded in the current account | Recorded in the capital account |

questions.stem_md: Snehal, a partner in an imagined firm in Nadiad, withdrew ₹15,000 on 1 June 2025, ₹10,000 on 1 November 2025 and ₹20,000 on 1 February 2026. Interest on drawings is 10% per annum and the year ends on 31 March 2026. Using the product method, find the interest (in ₹).

questions.solution_md: First drawing out 11 months, last 6; average = (11 + 6) ÷ 2 = 8½ months. Interest = 30,000 × 12/100 × 8.5/12 = ₹2,550.

questions.stem_md: The accountant of an imagined firm in Ballia is unsure whether rent paid to a partner and a partner's salary belong in the same account. Distinguish between a charge against profit and an appropriation of profit on two bases.
questions.solution_md: Any two bases; rent to a partner is a charge and a partner's salary is an appropriation.

answer.model_answer_md:
| Basis | Charge against profit | Appropriation of profit |
|---|---|---|
| Account | Debited to the Profit and Loss Account | Debited to the Profit and Loss Appropriation Account |
| Profit needed? | Allowed even if the firm makes a loss | Allowed only out of profit |
| Examples | Rent to a partner, interest on a partner's loan, manager's commission | Partner's salary, interest on capital, transfer to reserve |

questions.stem_md: Alok withdrew ₹15,000 at the **beginning** of every quarter of 2025-26 from an imagined printing firm in Gaya. Interest on drawings is 8% per annum. Calculate the interest on his drawings, showing the average period.
questions.solution_md: Average the months outstanding of the first and last drawing.

answer.model_answer_md:
Total drawings = ₹15,000 × 4 = ₹60,000. Drawings are out for 12, 9, 6 and 3 months; average period = (12 + 3) ÷ 2 = 7½ months.

Interest = ₹60,000 × 8/100 × 7.5/12 = **₹3,000**.

questions.stem_md: A partner draws an equal sum every month. Explain why interest on drawings is charged for an average period of 6½ months if he draws at the beginning of each month, but 5½ months if he draws at the end.
questions.solution_md: Average period = (months outstanding for the first drawing + for the last) ÷ 2.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Beginning of each month:** the first drawing (1 April) is out for 12 months and the last (1 March) for 1 month. Equal drawings at equal intervals average (12 + 1) ÷ 2 = 6½ months.
2. **End of each month:** the first drawing (30 April) is out for 11 months and the last (31 March) for none, so the average is (11 + 0) ÷ 2 = 5½ months.

questions.stem_md: Bharati, a partner in an imagined firm in Purnia, withdrew ₹20,000 on 1 May 2025, ₹12,000 on 31 July 2025, ₹18,000 on 1 October 2025 and ₹10,000 on 31 January 2026.
